sections.h2: Where does a Madison County deed get recorded?
sections.html:
In London, at the courthouse. The Madison County Recorder sits at 1 N Main St, Room 40, London, OH 43140, and takes calls at 740-852-1854. Hours are Monday through Friday, 8 AM to 4 PM, but the office stops recording at 3:30 PM, so a deed handed over at 3:45 waits until the next business day.

Electronic recording is available through four named platforms: CSC eRecording (866-652-0111), Simplifile, ePN and Hopdox. Ask your title company or attorney which platform they use, since the deed can then be recorded without a trip to the courthouse.

sections.h2: What is the recording fee in Madison County?
sections.html:
The Recorder's page states $39.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each additional page, effective January 1, 2025. It explains that Senate Bill 94 added a $5.00 surcharge to most documents to pay for preserving and digitizing records and for the office's ongoing costs, and it cites section 317.32 of the Revised Code.

That statute is where the structure of the fee comes from. For a standard instrument it sets a base fee and an equal housing trust fund fee on the first two pages, smaller per-page amounts after that, and an optional county preservation surcharge of up to five dollars. Copies, certifications, marginal references and zoning filings each carry their own listed amounts. Call 740-852-1854 for the current figure on any unusual document before you send payment.

sections.h2: How far back do Madison County's online land records reach?
sections.html:
Different record types start at different dates, according to the Recorder's own note. Checking the right category saves a trip to the courthouse:

Online coverage listed on the Madison County Recorder's page
Record typeCoverage stated
DeedsScanned, indexed and online from March 1, 1920 to present
Mortgages, indexingIndexed from July 17, 1964
Mortgages, imagesScanned and indexed from September 25, 1968
Miscellaneous, lease, lien, federal tax lien, mechanics lien, unemployment compensation lien, mortgage releaseHistorical Archive online, dating to at least 1980, some older

All the original books remain in the office. If a search turns up a gap, call the counter and ask staff to follow up in the books.

sections.h2: What does the Madison County Auditor do with a deed first?
sections.html:
Ohio makes the Auditor endorse the deed before the Recorder files it. Under section 319.202, the buyer's representative submits a statement of value, or a statement of the exemption reason, and the Auditor notes the conveyance fee on the deed itself.

The Madison County Auditor is at 1 N Main St, PO Box 47, London, OH 43140-0047, phone 740-852-9717, weekdays 8 AM to 4 PM. Its property transfer forms page lists the packet pieces a closer may need:

  • DTE 100, the conveyance fee statement of value and receipt.
  • DTE 100EX, the statement of the reason for an exemption.
  • DTE 101, a statement of conveyance of homestead property.
  • DTE 102, a statement of conveyance of current agricultural use valuation property.
  • DTE 100M and DTE 41 for manufactured or mobile homes.
  • Affidavits of trustee and successor trustee under sections 317.22 and 5302.171.

The Auditor's site also carries a conveyance fee calculator under its Tools menu. Run your sale through it, or phone the office, rather than guessing at the county's rate.

sections.h2: How does Ohio define the value used for a Madison County deed?
sections.html:
Section 319.202 spells it out. For an ordinary sale, value is the full consideration paid or to be paid, and that includes the amount of any mortgage or vendor's lien on the property. For a gift in whole or part, value is the price the property would bring on the open market between a willing buyer and willing seller. No one may willfully falsify the figure.

The same section adds two disclosures to the transfer packet. The buyer affirms that the seller was asked whether the taxes are being reduced under the homestead or owner-occupancy programs, and whether the land has been in the current agricultural use valuation. If the answer is yes, a sworn instrument must accompany the statement. When the property is residential rental property, the Auditor's endorsement also reminds the buyer to file landlord information under section 5323.02.

sections.h2: Which statutes control the conveyance fee on a Madison County sale?
sections.html:
Two sections matter. Section 319.54(G)(3) sets the statewide charge at one dollar, or ten cents for each $100 or fraction of it, whichever is larger, and lists the transfers that owe nothing. Section 322.02 allows a county to levy its own transfer tax, capped at thirty cents per $100 and paid by the grantor to the Auditor ahead of recording.

The first section also names the exempt cases. Several apply to estates and families:

  • A gift between spouses, or from a parent to a child.
  • A transfer between heirs of one decedent when nobody pays money.
  • A move into or out of a trust the grantor can revoke.
  • A deed to a surviving spouse under the statute on spousal sales of estate property.
  • A corrective deed that fixes an earlier recorded deed.

Whatever the reason, the exemption statement goes on the form.

sections.h2: What should a Madison County seller know about the county itself?
sections.html:
Madison County lies in central Ohio west of Franklin County, with London as the seat and largest city. Per Wikipedia, it covers 467 square miles, nearly all land, and belongs to the Columbus metropolitan area. Interstates 70 and 71 both run through it on their way to Columbus, and a small part of Dublin extends into the county.

QuickFacts puts Madison County at 46,985 residents in mid-2025, up 7.1 percent since the 2020 base, with 17,383 housing units. Over 2020 to 2024, a typical owned home was valued at $250,100 and a typical household earned $87,045. Owners occupy 77.5 percent of homes, rent runs a median $943, and the average commute is 24.9 minutes, which fits a county feeding workers into Columbus. The Auditor has also finished a countywide reappraisal for tax year 2026, with tentative values shown for each parcel on its website, so sellers should look up their own parcel before setting a price.

sections.h2: What is the history behind Madison County's records?
sections.html:
Madison County was established in 1810 and named for James Madison, and in 1850 its population was 10,015, mostly farming households. By 2020 it had 43,824 people. The county also hosts several state operations, including the Ohio Peace Officer Training Academy and the Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation, according to Wikipedia.

Neighbors include Union and Champaign counties to the north and northwest, Franklin County to the east, Pickaway to the southeast, Fayette to the south, and Greene and Clark to the west. Because of those borders, a Madison County seller sometimes owns a second parcel across a county line, and each county's recorder and auditor must handle their own part of the transfer.

faqs.q: What time does the Madison County Recorder stop accepting documents?
faqs.a: 3:30 PM. The office is open until 4 PM on weekdays but stops recording at 3:30, so deliver deeds earlier in the afternoon or use an e-recording service.

faqs.q: How much does the Madison County Recorder charge for a deed?
faqs.a: The Recorder lists $39.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each additional page, in effect since January 1, 2025. Check with the office for extra charges that apply to references, copies or special filings.

faqs.q: Can I e-record a deed in Madison County?
faqs.a: Yes. The Recorder names CSC eRecording, Simplifile, ePN and Hopdox as the electronic routes. Ask your title company or attorney which one they use.

faqs.q: Does the Madison County Auditor have a form for a trust or estate transfer?
faqs.a: Its forms page lists DTE 100EX for exemption reasons and affidavits for a trustee or successor trustee under Revised Code sections 317.22 and 5302.171. An attorney should pick the right ones for your situation.

faqs.q: How old are Madison County's scanned deeds?
faqs.a: Deeds are scanned, indexed and online from March 1, 1920 forward, according to the Recorder. Mortgages are scanned and indexed from September 25, 1968, and the original books stay in the office.
